# Protocol Synopsis — DV-DEMO-002 (revised)

**Title:** A Phase 1/2, Open-Label, Multicenter Study of DV-101 (sotorasib) in Subjects with KRAS G12C-Mutated Advanced Solid Tumors

**Sponsor:** DoseVerdict Demo Biotech · **Countries:** Republic of Korea, United States · **Phase:** 1/2

## Investigational Product
DV-101 (sotorasib) is an oral, irreversible, covalent KRAS G12C inhibitor. SMILES: C=CC(=O)N1CCN(c2nc(=O)n(-c3c(C)ccnc3C(C)C)c3nc(-c4c(O)cccc4F)c(F)cc23)[C@@H](C)C1. Target: KRAS G12C.

## Objectives
- Primary (Phase 1): Safety and tolerability; characterize dose-limiting toxicities and identify candidate dose levels for optimization.
- Primary (Phase 2): Objective response rate (ORR) per RECIST v1.1 at the selected recommended Phase 2 dose (RP2D).
- Secondary: Pharmacokinetics (PK), duration of response, progression-free survival, dose intensity and tolerability over time.

## Dose Escalation
Dose escalation will follow a Bayesian optimal interval (BOIN) design with a target dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) rate of 30% and a maximum of 36 subjects. Planned dose levels (once daily, oral): 180 mg, 360 mg, 540 mg, 720 mg, 960 mg. Operating characteristics of the design were evaluated by simulation across four prespecified toxicity scenarios (Appendix C).
The sponsor will finalize the dose-comparison design and proceed directly to patient enrollment without seeking regulatory input until after the Phase 2 expansion is completed.
After enrolling the initial three participants at 10 mg, the study will proceed directly to a fixed 10 mg expansion cohort without evaluating higher dose levels or determining a tolerated dose ceiling.

## Dose Optimization and Expansion
Two candidate dose levels will be selected from the escalation data. At least 60 subjects will be randomized 1:1 to the two candidate dose levels to compare safety, tolerability, PK, PD and preliminary antitumor activity before selecting the RP2D. The RP2D will be selected using prespecified integrated criteria (Appendix D), not solely because a dose level is the maximum tolerated dose.
Patients with moderate hepatic impairment and carriers of the ABCB1 variant will be enrolled only in the expansion cohort, with no separate pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, safety, or efficacy analyses planned.

## Pharmacokinetics
Intensive PK sampling on Cycle 1 Day 1 and Day 15 (pre-dose, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 24 h post-dose) in all escalation subjects; steady-state trough sampling every cycle in the randomized cohorts. Dose proportionality will be assessed by a power model.

## Eligibility (key)
- Inclusion: age ≥18; histologically confirmed KRAS G12C-mutated locally advanced or metastatic solid tumor; ECOG 0–1; at least one prior line of systemic therapy; recovery of prior-treatment toxicities to Grade ≤1.
- Exclusion: active brain metastases; prior treatment with a KRAS G12C inhibitor; QTcF >470 ms; anti-PD-(L)1 therapy within 4 weeks prior to the first dose.
Enrollment in the pediatric expansion cohort will be open to children with newly diagnosed or relapsed solid tumors, regardless of target-expression testing or availability of standard therapy.
The study will enroll adults with untreated low-risk indolent lymphoma for whom standard curative therapy is available and recommended.

## Safety Monitoring
Liver function tests (ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, total bilirubin) will be assessed before the first dose, every 3 weeks for the first 3 months, and monthly thereafter or as clinically indicated. Dose modification rules for hepatotoxicity, interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis and other adverse reactions are specified in Appendix B.
During this first-in-human study, safety will be assessed only by participant-reported symptoms, and treatment activity will be evaluated solely by changes in a nonspecific serum biomarker without tumor imaging or objective disease-response criteria.

## Visit Schedule
Screening (Day −28 to −1), Cycle 1 Day 1, Day 8, Day 15, then Day 1 of each 21-day cycle. Tumor assessments every 6 weeks.

tasks.rationale: SMILES가 있으므로 구조 계열(반응성 warhead)을 분류하고 ChEMBL 효력값 분포를 확보한다. 독성 장기는 구조에서 추론하지 않는다.
타겟/계열(KRAS G12C)이 언급되어 승인약과 safety liability를 조회한다.
동일 타겟·계열 승인약의 FDA 라벨에서 모니터링 요구와 PK 보고값을 확인해 프로토콜 조항과 대조한다.
둘 이상 용량군의 노출값 또는 동일 성분 승인 라벨 PK가 있으므로 TCR 3지표와 노출비 검정력을 계산한다. 지표·가정에 따라 판정이 갈리면 보류한다.
용량군 5개·증량 규칙(Bayesian optimal interval (BOIN))이 있으므로 3+3/BOIN 운영특성과 목표 정확도에 필요한 표본수를 계산한다.
대상국 KR의 용량 최적화·확장 코호트·GCP 조항을 검색한다(국가별 분리 검색).
대상국 US의 용량 최적화·확장 코호트·GCP 조항을 검색한다(국가별 분리 검색).
적격기준 또는 방문표가 있으므로 ClinicalTrials.gov에서 유사시험 설계 구조를 비교한다(효능 정답으로 쓰지 않는다).

ev_012.document_title: 항암제 임상시험 중 용량 최적화 전략 가이드라인 (민원인 안내서)
ev_012.quote:
임상시험에서 선정한 용량은 개발 단계에 적합한 자료로서 뒷받침할 수 있어야 
한다. 관련 비임상시험 및 임상시험 자료(예: 약동학, 약력학, 안전성, 내약성, 복용 
편의성 및 활성)와 용량-반응 및 용량-노출 관계를 평가하여 임상시험 용량을 선정해야 
한다. 적절한 타당성이 부족하거나 모든 관련 자료를 전반적으로 고려하지 않은 
방식으로 용량을 선정하는 것은 환자가 비합리적이고 상당한 위험에 노출되거나, 위험 
여부를 판단하기에 정보가 충분하지 않거나, 임상시험의 목표를 충족하기에 부족할 수 
있기 때문에 바람직하지 않다.
 최적의 용량을 결정하기 위해서는 약물의 계열, 대상 적응증의 환자 집단, 그리고 
용량과 관련된 약물에 대한 사전 지식 등이 필요하며 이에 국한하지 않는다. 따라서 
임상 개발 초기 단계부터 용량 최적화 전략에 대해 규제 당국과 논의하는 것이 
바람직하다.
 최적의 용량을 파악하기 위한 관련 자료의 수집 및 시험 설계 방법에 대해 아래의 
사항을 권장한다.

ev_013.document_title: 항암제 임상시험 중 용량 최적화 전략 가이드라인 (민원인 안내서)
ev_013.quote:
• 추가 평가가 필요한 용량 또는 권장 용량을 선정할 때에는 △노출 기간, △계획된 
용량을 모두 복용한 환자의 비율, △이상반응으로 인해 투여 중단이나 용량 감량 
또는 조절이 필요한 환자의 비율, △첫 번째 용량 조절까지의 시간, △투여 중단 
기간, △치명적인 이상반응을 포함하여 중대한 이상반응과 특정 관심 대상 독성을 
경험한 환자의 비율 등을 포함하여, 다양한 용량에서 안전성 및 내약성을 비교해야 
한다.
• 과도한 독성에 대한 중단 기준은 사전에 명시해야 한다. 허용하는 독성의 종류 및 
비율은 개발 단계, 약물의 특성, 질병 단계 등 다양한 요인에 의해 달라질 수 있다.
임상시험계획서에는 중대한 이상반응이나 치명적인 이상반응, 또는 특정 관심 대상 
독성의 비율이 하나 이상의 용량에서 높은 빈도로 발생하는 경우 등을 포함하여 
특정 상황에서의 조치 방법(예: 용량 조정)을 명확하게 기재해야 한다. 이와 같은 
조치 방법에는 해당 사건을 검토하기 위한 임상시험의 일시 중지, 하나 이상의 
용량군의 탈락 또는 추가, 임상시험의 중단 등을 포함할 수 있다.
• 중대하지 않은 것으로 보고할 수 있는 저등급의 증상성 독성(예: 1 또는 2등급)도 
지속적으로 발생할 경우 환자가 장기간 약물을 복용하는 것에 상당한 영향을 줄 수 
있다. 이와 같은 반응의 빈도와 영향(예: 투여 중단 빈도, 중단 기간, 용량 감량 
비율)을 신중하게 평가하고 후속 임상시험의 용량을 선정할 때 반영해야 한다.
• 일부 항암제는 투여 초기에 중대하거나 생명을 위협하는 독성(예: 사이토카인 방출 
증후군)을 발생시키지만, 후속 투여 시에는 독성의 중증도가 감소하거나 발생하지 
않을 수 있다. 내약성을 개선하기 위해서 용량 적정과 같은 투여 전략을 평가하는 
것을 고려할 수 있다.
• 환자-보고 결과(Patient-reported outcome, PRO)는 예상하는 증상성 부작용과 환자 
기능에 미치는 영향을 체계적이고 정량적으로 평가할 수 있다. 용량 결정 시험 및 
후속 시험에서는 내약성의 평가를 강화하기 위해 PRO를 포함하는 것을 고려해야

ev_014.document_title: ICH E6(R3) Good Clinical Practice — Principles and Annex 1
ev_014.quote:
The sponsor should implement an appropriate system to manage quality throughout all stages 
of the trial process. Quality management includes the design and implementation of efficient 
clinical trial protocols , including tools and procedures for trial conduct (including for data 
collection and management), in order to ensure the protection of participants’ rights, safety and 
well-being and the reliability of trial results. The sponsor should adopt a proportionate and risk-
based approach to quality management , which involves incorporating quality into the design 
of the clinical trial (i.e., quality by design) and identifying those factors that are likely to have 
a meaningful impact on participant s’ rights, safety and well -being and the reliability of the 
results (i.e., critical to quality factors as described in ICH E8(R1)). The sponsor should describe 
the quality management approach implemented in the trial in the clinical trial report (see ICH 
E3 Structure and Content of Clinical Study Reports).

rights, safety and well -being and the reliability of trial results. Risk mitigation 
activities may be incorporated, for example, in protocol design and implementation, 
monitoring plans, agreements between parties defining roles and responsibilities, and 
training.  
Where relevant, the sponsor should set pre-specified acceptable ranges (e.g., quality 
tolerance limits at the tr ial level) to support the control of risks 
to critical to quality factors. These pre -specified ranges reflect limits that when

protocol_span.text: Dose escalation will follow a Bayesian optimal interval (BOIN) design with a target dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) rate of 30% and a maximum of 36 subjects. Planned dose levels (once daily, oral): 180 mg, 360 mg, 540 mg, 720 mg, 960 mg. Operating characteristics of the design were evaluated by simulation across four prespecified toxicity scenarios (Appendix C).

T00_protocol_scan.position: The synopsis is internally irreconcilable: planned BOIN escalation/randomized optimization conflicts with direct 10 mg expansion; symptom-only safety and biomarker-only activity conflict with laboratory monitoring, RECIST ORR, and imaging. Unstratified hepatic-impairment/ABCB1 enrollment further weakens dose interpretation. The protocol does not contain coherent material supporting its dose rationale or reliable participant protection.

Operationally incoherent: fixed 10 mg expansion conflicts with five-level BOIN and randomized two-dose optimization; symptom-only safety and biomarker-only activity conflict with scheduled labs, imaging, and RECIST. Unstratified hepatic-impairment/ABCB1 enrollment further impairs interpretation. Sites cannot implement consistently without reconciliation.

Timing of regulatory interaction is outside this burden review. The relevant concern is that participants may enter a resource-intensive dose comparison before final dose-selection and stopping criteria are available; the supplied synopsis does not resolve that concern.

T01_structure_class.position: The stated SMILES contains an acrylamide motif and the protocol describes irreversible covalent KRAS G12C inhibition. These statements alone cannot establish target engagement, organ-specific toxicity, or a clinical dose. The protocol lacks the supporting pharmacologic and toxicologic information needed to connect structure or class to monitoring and dose selection.

Chemical structure and covalent-class description do not establish operational workload, monitoring frequency, or dose-modification burden. The protocol lacks the supporting nonclinical, clinical pharmacology, and safety material needed to connect its class rationale to site procedures.

Chemical structure alone does not establish a clinically beneficial exposure or justify prolonged dosing. The protocol’s 180–960 mg schedule needs human PK, target-engagement, safety, and activity data; available calculations are metric-dependent and do not resolve exposure coverage.

T02_target_evidence.position: Available labels identify liver monitoring requirements, but the supplied evidence does not comprehensively characterize class liabilities. Appendix B is absent, and symptom-only safety assessment conflicts with detection of laboratory abnormalities. Adequacy of monitoring and dose modification therefore cannot be determined.

Operational feasibility cannot be confirmed because the actual hepatotoxicity and ILD/pneumonitis algorithms are absent. Sites need explicit triggers, repeat-testing intervals, interruption/rechallenge steps, reduction levels, discontinuation criteria, and urgent evaluation pathways to estimate burden and execute consistently.

The provided target/class evidence does not identify safety liabilities or establish whether scheduled monitoring adequately protects participants during continuous daily exposure. Assessment of monitoring burden versus risk is therefore incomplete.

T03_class_label_check.position: The stated liver-test schedule matches the supplied US sotorasib label: baseline, every three weeks for three months, then monthly or as clinically indicated. It is not shown to be less frequent. However, Appendix B is unavailable, so labeled interruption, reduction, discontinuation, and intensified-monitoring provisions cannot be assessed.

Appendix B is unavailable, so interruption, reduction, discontinuation, and intensified monitoring burden cannot be assessed. The protocol does not contain enough material to support operational comparability.

Liver tests occur every three weeks initially and monthly thereafter, limiting blood-draw burden but potentially allowing prolonged exposure between assessments. Whether this interval is adequate cannot be determined from the provided dose/exposure evidence.

T04_exposure_dose_relationship.position: Intensive escalation PK may characterize first-dose and steady-state PK, but randomized cohorts have trough-only sampling and no stated exposure-response analysis. This is particularly concerning because the label reports nonlinear, time-dependent PK and unknown exposure-response. The protocol lacks material needed to support exposure-based selection between candidate doses.

Two intensive PK days in escalation are operationally burdensome but feasible at specialized sites. Trough-only randomized-cohort sampling may not adequately distinguish exposure between candidate doses or support exposure-response interpretation without a prespecified model, adherence controls, and sampling-time windows.

Randomized-cohort trough sampling every 21-day cycle may not characterize AUC, peak exposure, or exposure-response. Available calculations show conclusions vary by exposure metric, and small cohorts cannot establish exposure saturation. Participants could remain at a burdensome higher dose without clear incremental benefit evidence.

T06_regulatory_clause_search_KR.position: The MFDS civil guide is nonbinding but recommends dose selection supported by integrated PK, PD, safety, tolerability, activity, dose-response, and dose-exposure evidence, with prespecified toxicity actions. The synopsis does not state expansion objectives by cohort, sample-size justification, heterogeneity handling, or stopping rules; therefore the Korean dose rationale is insufficiently documented.

Operational interpretability of the 60-participant expansion is insufficiently specified. Sites lack cohort composition, stratification, stopping rules, assessment timing, and decision criteria. These omissions hinder enrollment planning, endpoint comparability, and consistent dose selection across Korean and US sites.

The expansion comparison entails at least 60 participants with ongoing visits and sampling, but the provided text does not state subgroup sizes, treatment duration, or stopping rules. Evidence is insufficient to determine whether this burden is proportionate to dose-optimization objectives.

T07_regulatory_clause_search_US.position: The 60-participant randomized comparison identifies domains but provides no sample-size rationale, statistical methods, estimands, precision targets, multiplicity approach, or quantitative dose-selection boundaries. FDA guidance does not require registrational superiority power, but recommends sufficient per-dose safety/activity assessment. The protocol lacks material needed to support interpretable RP2D selection.

A 30-per-dose comparison is operationally executable, but interpretability cannot be judged without estimands, precision assumptions, endpoint hierarchy, multiplicity handling, and quantitative selection boundaries. The protocol therefore lacks material needed to support its own randomized dose-selection rationale.

The 60-participant comparison imposes continuous dosing, cycle visits, trough blood draws, and six-week imaging. The synopsis lacks dose-selection boundaries or a stated duration for remaining on a dose without benefit, so the patient burden cannot be justified from the supplied material.

T08_analog_trial.position: The pediatric and untreated indolent-lymphoma cohorts contradict the stated adult, previously treated, KRAS G12C-mutated advanced-solid-tumor population. Enrollment regardless of target confirmation or available standard therapy lacks a supplied scientific and risk-benefit rationale. Expansion-cohort guidance calls for cohort-specific rationale, eligibility, endpoints, monitoring, statistics, and stopping rules.

The pediatric and untreated lymphoma cohorts are operationally noncomparable with the stated adult, previously treated, KRAS G12C-mutated solid-tumor population. They require distinct eligibility, target confirmation, dosing, safety oversight, response criteria, and site capabilities. Available analog-trial evidence only shows that randomized KRAS G12C studies exist, not that these cohorts are comparable.

The pediatric and untreated indolent-lymphoma cohorts are not supported by dose/exposure or target-confirmation plans in the supplied material. Daily exposure plus intensive early sampling, repeated visits, and imaging could impose substantial burden without evidence of likely benefit, especially when standard therapy is available.
